study_identification.title: A neuroimaging measure to capture heterogeneous patterns of atrophy in Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies

study_characteristics.study_objective: To quantify patterns of neurodegenerative dissimilarity in participants with Parkinson's disease (PD) and Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) using neuroanatomical normative modelling, and to evaluate the potential clinical relevance of total outlier count by testing its association with key clinical measures in PD and DLB.

dataset_name.reason: The paper clearly states that the reference normative model was developed by Rutherford et al., 2022, using a large cohort of 58,836 participants from 82 sites. The dataset name is clearly identified by referencing the original publication.
dataset_name.supporting_text: Rutherford and colleagues (Rutherford et al., 2022) modelled normative lifespan curves for cortical thicknesses across 148 regions (Destrieux parcellation) and subcortical volumes derived from Freesurfer using a warped Bayesian Linear Regression with age and sex as covariates, and accounting for site differences (Bayer et al., 2022). Bayesian linear regression with likelihood warping allows accurate modelling of non-Gaussian effects and upscaling of normative models to large cohorts (Fraza et al., 2021). Their reference cohort comprised 58,836 participants from 82 sites.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Linear regressions adjusting for age and sex were used to test: (1) group differences in total outlier count between high and low visual performers with PD, and between DLB and PD; (2) associations between total outlier count and cognitive measures (composite cognitive score, MoCA, Hooper Visual Organisation Test) and disease-specific measures (MDS-UPDRS, MDS-UPDRS-III, UM-PDHQ, HADS depression) in PD and DLB groups separately. Mann-Whitney U tests were used to compare median Hamming distance scores between groups. Group comparisons for proportion of outliers at each region were conducted using Mann-Whitney U tests and corrected for multiple comparisons using False Discovery Rate (FDR). A conventional General Linear Model (GLM) approach using FreeSurfer was used to test for regional group-level differences in cortical thickness between high and low visual performers with PD and between PD and DLB, with age and sex as covariates and Monte Carlo multiple comparison correction (threshold p<0.05). Sensitivity analyses were performed using a more liberal outlier threshold (z-score < -1.282) and with exclusion of potential outlying participants.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Neuroanatomical normative modelling revealed significantly greater total outlier count and inter-individual dissimilarity in DLB compared with PD, and in PD low visual performers (at-risk for dementia) compared to high visual performers; total outlier count was significantly associated with cognitive performance in both DLB and PD, whereas conventional GLM analyses failed to identify differences between PD visual performance groups.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Mean total outlier count was significantly higher in DLB (n=61, mean=8.7, SD=11.3) compared to PD (n=108, mean=3.60, SD=6.0) after adjusting for age and sex (β=-5.60, SE=1.74, t=-3.23, p<0.01), and higher in PD low visual performers (n=34, mean=5.4, SD=8.7) compared to high visual performers (n=62, mean=2.3, SD=3.5) (β=-4.73, SE=1.30, t=-3.64, p<0.01). DLB participants from NACC (n=25) had significantly higher numbers of outliers compared to UCL (n=36) after adjusting for age and sex (β=-6.02, SE=2.97, t=-2.02, p=0.050). Dissimilarity measured by Hamming distance was significantly higher in PD low visual performers (n=34, mean=7.1, SD=8.4) compared to high visual performers (n=62, mean=3.3, SD=3.4) (W=522.5, p<0.01), and higher in DLB (n=61, mean=12.6, SD=10.3) compared to PD (n=108, mean=4.6, SD=6.0) (W=5649, p<0.01). In the PD group, 125 out of 169 regions had at least one patient with an outlier, compared with 147/169 regions in DLB. The region with highest outliers in PD was left paracentral lobule and sulcus (n=15, 13.9%), while in DLB it was right posterior-dorsal cingulate gyrus (n=15, 24.6%). In DLB (UCL site only, n=36), higher total outlier count was significantly associated with poorer composite cognitive score (β=-2.01, SE=0.79, t=-2.54, p=0.02) and MoCA (β=-0.55, SE=0.27, t=-2.04, p=0.05), but not with Hooper Visual Organisation Test (β=-0.45, SE=0.24, t=-1.89, p=0.068). In PD (n=108), higher total outlier count was significantly associated with poorer visuoperception measured by Hooper Visual Organisation Test (β=-0.67, SE=0.19, t=-3.59, p<0.01), but not with composite cognitive score (β=-1.19, SE=0.79, t=-1.51, p=0.14) or MoCA (β=-0.17, SE=0.31, t=-0.55, p=0.58). No associations were found between total outlier count and disease-specific measures (MDS-UPDRS, MDS-UPDRS-III, UM-PDHQ, HADS) in either group. A conventional GLM approach did not find significant clusters of differences in cortical thickness between high and low visual performers in PD. Comparing PD with DLB, GLM found two significant clusters in left precentral region and one in right superior frontal and precentral regions, indicating reduced cortical thickness in DLB. Sensitivity analyses with a more liberal threshold (z-score<-1.282) and with exclusion of outlying participants showed qualitatively similar results.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Outliers were defined using a threshold of z-score <-1.96, which may fail to capture potentially relevant subthreshold levels of neurodegeneration, though results were similar with alternative thresholds and mean cortical thickness z-score. There were significant differences between DLB data collection sites: UCL data were collected prospectively with study aims in mind, while NACC is a large relational database where neuropsychological and clinical information was limited. NACC participants had longer disease duration (UCL: 3.7±2.0 years, NACC: 5.3±3.3 years), which may partly account for observed increased total outlier count in that group. Alternative explanations include differences in study inclusion criteria and selection bias of less functionally impaired participants at UCL due to testing demands. MRI scans from NACC were performed on 1.5T scanners while UCL used 3T scanners, though the normative modeling pipeline with transfer learning is designed to account for such differences. The DLB dataset is relatively small (n=61), which may have underpowered correlational analyses in the DLB group; DLB patients are generally frailer and more challenging to assess. Three participants (one PD, two DLB) had much higher total outlier counts (45, 50, 53) than other participants (PD range: 0-24, DLB: 0-38); their imaging showed no significant structural abnormalities, acquisition, or processing errors, and clinical assessment was consistent with unambiguous diagnoses, but results are presented with and without these participants. The study used visual performance to stratify PD rather than MCI status because PD-MCI phenomenology is heterogeneous and many patients revert to normal cognition within five years.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The study demonstrates that neuroanatomical normative modelling can overcome limitations of group-average analyses in heterogeneous disorders like PD and DLB. Total outlier count is agnostic to the regional location of cortical atrophy, whereas conventional GLM approaches require cortical atrophy to be in the same locations between individuals. The methodology yields personalized measures rather than traditional case-control group average measures and holds promise for prognosis or treatment-response predictions for individual patients. The authors suggest that total outlier count may have clinical utility as a prognostic neuroimaging measure of disease progression in Lewy body disorders, as has been shown in Alzheimer's disease. Importantly, total outlier count can be calculated based on cortical thicknesses and subcortical volumes from freely-available automated pipelines (FreeSurfer) for commonly acquired T1w-MRI scans. The Hamming distance enabled quantification of dissimilarity between groups, revealing greater inter-individual heterogeneity in low compared to high visual performers with PD, and in DLB compared to PD, consistent with previous work in Alzheimer's disease. Normative modelling has advantages over W-score approaches: the reference dataset (58,836) is around 1000-fold larger than most W-score reference datasets, capturing much greater population variability and providing more robust estimates of deviation; the pipeline enables inter-individual heterogeneity to be quantified, which is not usually examined using W-score approaches. Greater dissimilarity in DLB compared to PD may relate to greater cortical involvement in DLB. The lack of relationship between cognitive measures and total outlier count in PD may be due to ceiling effects in MoCA and composite cognitive scores, while the Hooper test measuring visuoperceptual processing may be particularly sensitive as these domains are affected early in PD.

general_notes.general_notes: This study applies a pre-trained normative model from Rutherford et al., 2022 (Elife 11: Charting brain growth and aging at high spatial precision) to clinical populations with Parkinson's disease and Dementia with Lewy bodies. The study is part of the Vision in Parkinson's disease study (PI: Dr. Weil, Queen Square Ethics Committee reference 15/LO/00476). PD participants were stratified into high and low visual performers based on performance on two computerised visual tasks: biological motion perception and the 'Cats-and-dogs' task (see Supplementary material). These tasks have been described previously (Zarkali et al., 2021; Weil et al., 2017; Weil et al., 2018; Leyland et al., 2020) and shown to predict dementia and poor outcomes in Parkinson's (Zarkali et al., 2021; Hannaway et al., 2023). Low visual performers performed worse than group median on both tasks. The study used data from two sites: University College London (UCL: 108 PD, 36 DLB, 38 controls) and NACC ADRC '8361' (25 DLB, 127 controls). UCL controls were recruited from spouses of patients and UCL volunteer databases, aged 50-80, with no past neurological or psychiatric history or cognitive impairment. NACC participants met criteria: dementia diagnosis, Lewy body disease as primary/contributing cause, not MCI, no PD diagnosis, and no cognitive impairment for controls. The study included 169 brain regions total (148 cortical from Destrieux parcellation and 21 subcortical from aseg.stats). In the PD group, 125 out of 169 regions had at least one patient with an outlier, compared with 147/169 regions in the DLB group. The region with the highest number of PD outliers was the left paracentral lobule and sulcus region (n=15, 13.9%), while in DLB it was the right posterior-dorsal part of the cingulate gyrus (dPCC) (n=15, 24.6%). The authors note that normative modelling has key advantages over W-score approaches, including a much larger reference dataset (58,836 vs typically dozens in W-score studies) providing more robust estimates and the ability to quantify inter-individual heterogeneity. The study performed sensitivity analyses with a more liberal outlier threshold (z-score <-1.282) and with exclusion of potential outlying participants (one PD with total outlier count 45, two DLB with counts 50 and 53), finding qualitatively similar results in both cases. Clinical measures were comprehensive: MMSE, MoCA, composite cognitive score (combining Stroop colour, letter fluency, category fluency, word recognition, Hooper test, and MoCA z-scores), Hooper Visual Organisation Test (visuoperceptual ability), MDS-UPDRS (global severity), MDS-UPDRS-III (motor function), UM-PDHQ (hallucinations), and HADS (depression). Statistical analyses were performed in R v4.2.2.
